learningObjectives.title: Deciduous woodlands or other biome management

questions.q: Which two climatic factors are the main influence on the global distribution of large-scale ecosystems (biomes)?
options: Temperature and precipitation
Altitude and soil colour
Wind speed and cloud type
Ocean salinity and tides
questions.explain: Global biome distribution is controlled chiefly by climate, especially temperature and rainfall, which vary with latitude.

questions.q: Where are tropical rainforests mainly located?
options: Around the Equator, between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn
Within the Arctic and Antarctic circles
Along the west coasts of continents at 40 to 60 degrees north
In the centres of large continents in the mid-latitudes
questions.explain: Tropical rainforests are concentrated near the Equator where it is hot and wet all year.

questions.q: Which biome is characterised by permafrost and low-growing vegetation such as mosses and lichens?
options: Tundra
Tropical rainforest
Hot desert
Temperate grassland
questions.explain: The tundra has a cold climate with permanently frozen subsoil (permafrost) that restricts plants to low-growing species.

questions.q: Which biome experiences distinct wet and dry seasons and is dominated by grasses with scattered trees?
options: Tropical grassland (savanna)
Deciduous woodland
Coniferous forest (taiga)
Tropical rainforest
questions.explain: Tropical grasslands, or savanna, lie between rainforests and deserts and have a marked dry season.

questions.q: Why do temperatures generally decrease as you move from the Equator towards the poles?
options: Insolation is spread over a larger area at higher latitudes
The Earth is closer to the Sun at the Equator
There is more land at the poles to absorb heat
Winds only blow from the poles to the Equator
questions.explain: At high latitudes the Sun's rays strike at a lower angle, spreading energy over a wider area and reducing warmth.

questions.q: Why do tropical rainforests have such high biodiversity?
options: Constant hot, wet conditions allow year-round plant growth
The climate has a long cold season that limits competition
Poor soils force species to specialise into just a few types
Frequent fires clear the land and encourage new growth
questions.explain: Uniformly hot and wet conditions all year support continuous growth and a huge variety of niches and species.

questions.q: In the rainforest nutrient cycle, where is the largest store of nutrients found?
options: In the biomass (living vegetation)
In the soil
In the litter layer
In the atmosphere
questions.explain: In tropical rainforests most nutrients are locked up in the dense living biomass rather than the thin soil.

questions.q: Why are tropical rainforest soils typically nutrient-poor despite the lush vegetation?
options: Heavy rainfall leaches nutrients from the soil
The soil is permanently frozen
There is too little rainfall to weather rock
Cold temperatures stop decomposition
questions.explain: Intense rainfall washes soluble nutrients down through the soil (leaching), leaving it infertile below the surface.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the 'drip tips' found on many rainforest leaves?
options: To allow heavy rainfall to run off quickly
To store water during dry spells
To reflect sunlight away from the plant
To trap insects for extra nutrients
questions.explain: Drip tips channel water off the leaf, preventing the growth of fungi and moulds in the humid climate.

questions.q: How do buttress roots help tall rainforest trees?
options: They give extra support in thin, shallow soils
They store water for the dry season
They absorb sunlight for photosynthesis
They release nutrients directly into the air
questions.explain: Large buttress roots spread out to stabilise tall trees whose roots cannot go deep into the shallow soil.

questions.q: Which of these is a major direct cause of tropical deforestation in the Amazon?
options: Clearing land for cattle ranching
Expansion of the tundra
Rising sea levels
Coppicing of native trees
questions.explain: Cattle ranching is the single largest cause of Amazon deforestation, with forest cleared to create pasture.

questions.q: How does large-scale deforestation tend to affect the local water cycle?
options: It reduces evapotranspiration, lowering local rainfall
It increases rainfall by adding moisture to the air
It has no effect on the water cycle
It permanently freezes the soil
questions.explain: Fewer trees means less water returned to the air by transpiration, which can reduce local rainfall over time.

questions.q: How does deforestation contribute to the enhanced greenhouse effect?
options: Burning and clearing trees releases stored carbon dioxide
Trees are replaced by ice that reflects heat
It removes methane from the atmosphere
It increases the amount of ozone in the stratosphere
questions.explain: Trees store carbon; clearing and burning them releases CO2 and removes a carbon sink, adding to global warming.

questions.q: What does 'selective logging' as a sustainable management strategy involve?
options: Felling only certain mature trees and leaving the rest
Clearing all trees in an area at once
Burning the forest to plant crops
Planting a single species of tree
questions.explain: Selective logging removes only chosen trees, allowing the forest structure and ecosystem to recover.

questions.q: A rainforest region introduces guided wildlife tours where fees fund conservation and local jobs. Which strategy is this?
options: Ecotourism
Cattle ranching
Monoculture plantation
Open-cast mining
questions.explain: Ecotourism generates income from conserving the forest, giving people a reason to protect rather than clear it.

questions.q: A company clears native rainforest and replants it entirely with oil palm. What is the most likely effect on biodiversity?
options: Biodiversity falls because a monoculture supports fewer species
Biodiversity rises because more trees are planted
Biodiversity is unaffected by the change
Biodiversity rises because soils become richer
questions.explain: Replacing a diverse forest with a single-crop monoculture destroys habitats and sharply reduces biodiversity.

questions.q: In which climatic zone are temperate deciduous woodlands found?
options: Mid-latitude temperate regions such as the UK
Equatorial regions with no seasons
Polar regions with permafrost
Arid desert regions
questions.explain: Deciduous woodlands grow in temperate mid-latitudes that have four distinct seasons and moderate rainfall.

questions.q: Why do deciduous trees drop their leaves in autumn and winter?
options: To reduce water loss when it is cold and water may be frozen
To attract more insects during the winter
To increase photosynthesis in the dark months
To make room for permafrost to form
questions.explain: Shedding leaves cuts transpiration and protects trees during winter when soil water can be frozen and unavailable.

questions.q: Which of these is a typical tree species of a British deciduous woodland?
options: Oak
Mahogany
Cactus
Scots pine only
questions.explain: Oak, along with species such as beech and ash, is characteristic of temperate deciduous woodlands in Britain.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes the vertical structure of a deciduous woodland from top to bottom?
options: Canopy, under-canopy, shrub layer, ground layer
Ground layer, shrub layer, canopy, under-canopy
Shrub layer, ground layer, canopy, under-canopy
Under-canopy, ground layer, shrub layer, canopy
questions.explain: Deciduous woodlands are layered from the tallest canopy down through the under-canopy and shrubs to the ground layer.

questions.q: A woodland manager cuts trees down to their base so that new shoots grow back for repeated harvesting. What is this traditional technique called?
options: Coppicing
Clear-felling
Leaching
Slash and burn
questions.explain: Coppicing cuts trees to the stump to encourage regrowth, providing a sustainable, renewable supply of wood.

questions.q: Why does the ground layer of a deciduous woodland often flower in early spring?
options: Light reaches the floor before the canopy leaves grow
The soil is warmest in mid-winter
The canopy blocks all light in spring
There is no rainfall in spring
questions.explain: Ground plants such as bluebells flower early to exploit the light before the canopy leafs out and shades them.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Geography B (1GB0) specification; Ecosystems, Biodiversity & Management
